claim: Sleep associated memory consolidation and reactivation play an important role in language acquisition and learning of new words.
source: Sleep associated memory consolidation and reactivation play an important role in language acquisition and learning of new words.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: TMR of easy words improved their overnight memory performance.
source: Here, we found that TMR of the easy words improved their overnight memory performance, whereas TMR of the difficult words had no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study, specifically the behavioral results showing significant overnight increases in d' values for high-PP cued words.

claim: TMR of difficult words had no effect on overnight memory performance.
source: Here, we found that TMR of the easy words improved their overnight memory performance, whereas TMR of the difficult words had no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in memory performance for low-PP cued words.

claim: Slow wave density increased independent of word difficulty following TMR presentations.
source: By comparing EEG activities after TMR presentations, we found an increase in slow wave density independent of word difficulty
evidence: This is supported by EEG data analysis showing significant increases in slow wave density after stimulus onset regardless of phonotactic probability condition.

claim: Spindle-band power nested during slow wave up-states was significantly higher in the easy/effective compared to the difficult/ineffective condition.
source: whereas the spindle-band power nested during the slow wave up-states – as an assumed underlying activity of memory reactivation – was significantly higher in the easy/effective compared to the difficult/ineffective condition.
evidence: This is supported by time-frequency EEG analysis showing significant cluster differences in spindle-band power during slow wave up-states between high-PP and low-PP conditions.

claim: Word learning difficulty by phonotactics impacts the effectiveness of TMR.
source: Our findings indicate that word learning difficulty by phonotactics impacts the effectiveness of TMR
evidence: This is supported by the differential behavioral outcomes between high-PP and low-PP word conditions following TMR.

claim: Prior encoding depth plays a critical role in sleep associated memory reactivation.
source: and further emphasize the critical role of prior encoding depth in sleep associated memory reactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between encoding performance differences (as measured by alpha desynchronization) and subsequent TMR effectiveness.

claim: Artificial words with similar phonotactic properties to real words are easier to learn and to remember.
source: Previous studies have shown that artificial words with similar phonotactic properties to real words are easier to learn and to remember (Frisch et al., 2000; Gupta and Tisdale, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pre-existing knowledge about sound structure (schemas) facilitates encoding and consolidation of new words.
source: suggesting that pre-existing knowledge about the sound structure (i.e. schemas) facilitates encoding and consolidation of new words.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on phonotactic properties and learning.

claim: A synchronized interplay between the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and unimodal associative cortices is proposed to explain schema instantiation and schema mnemonic effects at the neural level.
source: A synchronized interplay between the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and unimodal associative cortices is proposed to explain schema instantiation and schema mnemonic effects (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017) at the neural level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Learning of new words comprises a first stage of rapid initial familiarization represented by neural activities of the medial temporal lobe and a second stage of slow offline consolidation of the neocortex.
source: According to the complementary system account by Gaskell and colleagues (Davis and Gaskell, 2009; McClelland et al., 1995), learning of new words comprises a first stage of rapid initial familiarization represented by neural activities of the medial temporal lobe and a second stage of slow offline consolidation of the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is based on the complementary system account model cited in the text.

claim: After initial hippocampal learning, through sleep consolidation memory representations, the words are gradually integrated into long-term lexical and phonological memory structures of the neocortex.
source: The model suggests that, after initial hippocampal learning, through sleep consolidation memory representations, the words are gradually integrated into long-term lexical and phonological memory structures of the neocortex.
evidence: This is based on the complementary system account model.

claim: Memory consolidation processes might depend on spontaneous and repeated reactivation of newly formed memory traces during non-rapid eye-movement (NREM) sleep.
source: Additionally, these processes of memory consolidation might depend on spontaneous and repeated reactivation of the newly formed memory traces during non-rapid eye-movement (NREM) sleep (Rasch and Born, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a speculative element ('might depend').

claim: The active system consolidation hypothesis proposes synchronized hippocampal sharp-wave-ripples, thalamocortical sleep spindles and slow oscillations of NREM sleep as underlying activities of memory reactivation.
source: The active system consolidation hypothesis proposes synchronized hippocampal sharp-wave-ripples, thalamocortical sleep spindles and slow oscillations of NREM sleep as underlying activities of memory reactivation.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the active system consolidation hypothesis.

claim: Sleep spindles and hippocampal sharp wave ripples occur grouped during slow oscillations.
source: Accordingly, studies in humans Mölle et al., 2011; Cox et al., 2014; Staresina et al., 2015 and in rodent models Siapas and Wilson, 1998; Sirota and Buzsáki, 2005 found that sleep spindles and hippocampal sharp wave ripples occur grouped during slow oscillations
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to human and rodent studies.

claim: Sleep spindle and sharp wave ripple events correlate with memory consolidation.
source: and that these events correlate with memory consolidation (Rasch and Born, 2013; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Buzsáki, 1989; Girardeau and Zugaro, 2011; Singer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sleep-associated improvements in memory recognition were only observable for L2 words (Hungarian) but not L1 words (Spanish) in the Havas et al. study.
source: For example, Havas and co-authors (Havas et al., 2018) tested learning and consolidation of artificial words phonologically derived either from participant's native language (L1 words in Spanish) or foreign language (L2 words in Hungarian). Here, sleep-associated improvements in memory recognition were only observable in the condition of the L2 words
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: Reduced similarity to pre-existing knowledge facilitates consolidation during sleep.
source: suggesting that a reduced similarity to pre-existing knowledge facilitates consolidation during sleep.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Havas et al. study results.

claim: Sleep-associated memory benefits occurred only for semantically unrelated word-pairs, but not for semantically related words in the Payne et al. study.
source: Also, in a study by Payne et al., 2012, sleep-associated memory benefits occurred only for semantically unrelated word-pairs, but not for semantically related words.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: Sleep facilitated consolidation in a second language learning task in participants with a higher degree of meta-linguistic knowledge.
source: On the other hand, Zion et al., 2019 reported that sleep facilitated consolidation in a second language learning task in participants with a higher degree of meta-linguistic knowledge
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: Only schema-conformant but not non-conformant learnings benefitted from sleep in the Durrant et al. study.
source: Similarly, Durrant et al., 2015 reported that only schema-conformant but not non-conformant learnings benefitted from sleep.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: German-participants learning unknown Dutch vocabulary profited more from sleep compared to native French speakers when given the same amount of learning trials.
source: In a study from our own lab, German-participants learning unknown Dutch vocabulary profited more from sleep compared to native French speaker when given the same amount of learning trials
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a study from the authors' lab.

claim: TMR has been related to elevated slow-wave and spindle activity following cueing presentations as neural markers of memory reactivation.
source: TMR has been related to elevated slow-wave and spindle activity following cueing presentations as neural markers of memory reactivation (Cairney et al., 2018; Antony et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous TMR studies.

claim: TMR improved memory performance for associations between pseudo-words and familiar objects, but not for word associations of new/unknown objects in the Groch et al. study.
source: Groch and colleagues (Groch et al., 2017) reported improved memory performance by TMR for associations between pseudo-words and familiar objects, but not for word associations of new/unknown objects.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: Subjects showed better encoding performance for familiar compared to unknown objects before sleep in the Groch et al. study.
source: Here, before sleep, subjects showed as well better encoding performance for the familiar compared to the unknown objects.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: The effectiveness of TMR correlated positively with the initial encoding performance prior to sleep in the Creery et al. study.
source: In another study, Creery et al., 2015 of learning sound-object locations, the effectiveness of TMR correlated positively with the initial encoding performance prior to sleep.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: Both the Groch et al. and Creery et al. studies found significant associations between TMR's effectiveness and sleep spindle activities after the cueing presentations.
source: Additionally, both studies Groch et al., 2017; Creery et al., 2015 found significant associations between TMR's effectiveness and sleep spindle activities after the cueing presentations.
evidence: This claim is based on citations to two specific studies.

claim: Higher similarity between the learning material and the pre-existing knowledge facilitates reactivation and consolidation during sleep.
source: These findings suggest that higher similarity between the learning material and the pre-existing knowledge facilitates reactivation and consolidation during sleep.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: Reward related information has a beneficial effect on sleep-dependent memory consolidation and reactivation.
source: To consider the beneficial effect of reward related information on sleep-dependent memory consolidation and reactivation (Asfestani et al., 2020; Fischer and Born, 2009; Lansink et al., 2009; Sterpenich et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Four sets of artificial words were created consisting of different sequences of two vowels and two consonants.
source: We formed four sets of artificial words (40 words per set; see Supplementary files 1 and 2) consisting of different sequences of two vowels and two consonants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimulus creation.

claim: Significant differences in phonotactic probability exist between word sets G1/G2 and G3/G4.
source: Comparison analyses between the sets revealed significant differences in phonotactic probability (PP; Figure 1b; unpaired t-tests: G1 /G2>G3/G4, p<0.005, values of Cohen's d>0.71).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the phonotactic probability data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: PP quantifies the frequency of a single phoneme or a sequence of phonemes within a language and serves as a measurement of similarity between artificial words and pre-existing real word knowledge.
source: PP quantifies the frequency of a single phoneme (phoneme probabilities) or a sequence of phonemes (e.g. biphone probabilities) within a language and thus serves as a measurement of the similarity between the artificial words and the pre-existing real word knowledge.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in phonology.

claim: The high-PP condition consisted of 40 rewarded and 40 unrewarded words.
source: Therefore, the high- and the low-PP condition, consisted of 40 rewarded and 40 unrewarded words.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The low-PP condition consisted of 40 rewarded and 40 unrewarded words.
source: Therefore, the high- and the low-PP condition, consisted of 40 rewarded and 40 unrewarded words.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A repeated-measure ANOVA on d' revealed significant main effects of PP (F(1,32) = 5.13, p=0.03, η2=0.14).
source: A repeated-measure ANOVA on d' with PP (high vs. low) and presentations (1–3) as within-subjects factors revealed significant main effects of PP (F(1,32) = 5.13, p=0.03, η2=0.14)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the encoding performance analysis.

claim: A repeated-measure ANOVA on d' revealed significant main effects of presentations (F(2,64) = 95.67, p<0.001, η2=0.75).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the encoding performance analysis.

claim: Pairwise comparisons between PP conditions showed significant differences after the second presentation (t(32) = 2.35, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.41).
source: Additional pairwise comparisons between PP conditions showed significant differences after the first presentation (paired t-tests of the three presentations in order: (1) t(32) = 0.73, p=0.47; (2) t(32) = 2.35, p=0.03, Cohen's d=0.41
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis of encoding performance.

claim: Pairwise comparisons between PP conditions showed significant differences after the third presentation (t(32) = 2.17, p=0.04, Cohen's d=0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis of encoding performance.

claim: Superior learning performance was observed for words with high- compared to words with low-PP.
source: These results indicate superior learning performance for words with high- compared to words with low-PP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the encoding performance data.

claim: Time-frequency analyses revealed a strong desynchronization after word presentations (0.7–1.9 s to stimulus onset) in the frequency range of the alpha waves (8–13 Hz).
source: This analysis revealed a strong desynchronization after word presentations (0.7–1.9 s to stimulus onset) in the frequency range of the alpha waves (8–13 Hz) and pronounced over parietal and occipital electrodes in contrast to baseline activity (−1 to –0.1 s to stimulus onset; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by time-frequency EEG analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Alpha desynchronization was pronounced over parietal and occipital electrodes.
source: and pronounced over parietal and occipital electrodes in contrast to baseline activity
evidence: This is supported by topographic analysis of EEG data.

claim: A repeated-measure ANOVA on alpha power values revealed a significant increase in alpha desynchronization over presentations (F(2,64) = 4.19, p=0.02, η2=0.12).
source: Testing whether changes in alpha desynchronization correspond to increased encoding performance over repetitive presentations, a repeated-measure ANOVA on alpha power values merged over central electrodes (Pz, Cz) including presentations (1–3) as a single within-subjects factor revealed a significant increase in alpha desynchronization (F(2,64) = 4.19, p=0.02, η2=0.12).
evidence: This is a statistical result from EEG analysis during encoding.

claim: Cluster-based statistics of the third presentation revealed a significant cluster over the left posterior electrodes with stronger alpha power decrease for high- in contrast to low-PP condition.
source: Cluster-based statistics of the third presentation revealed a significant cluster over the left posterior electrodes with a stronger alpha power decrease for the high- in contrast to the low-PP condition (time window: 0.7–1.9 s; frequency range 8–13 Hz; averaged t-value over the five cluster electrodes = –2.69, p=0.01, Cohen's d=–0.48; Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by cluster-based permutation statistics on EEG data.

claim: A post-hoc repeated-measure ANOVA on alpha power changes revealed a main effect of PP (F(1,32) = 5.42, p=0.03, η2=0.15).
source: A post-hoc repeated-measure ANOVA on alpha power changes (merged over Pz and Cz electrodes) with PP (high vs. low) and presentations (2–3) as within-subjects factors revealed a main effect of PP (F(1,32) = 5.42, p=0.03, η2=0.15)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc EEG analysis.

claim: A post-hoc repeated-measure ANOVA on alpha power changes revealed a significant interaction (F(1,32) = 7.38, p=0.01, η2=0.19).
source: and a significant interaction (F(1,32) = 7.38, p=0.01, η2=0.19; Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc EEG analysis.

claim: Post-hoc pairwise comparison between PP conditions showed significant difference of the third presentation (t(32) = –3.55, p=0.001, Cohen's d=–0.62).
source: Additional post-hoc pairwise comparison between PP conditions showed significant difference of the third presentation (paired t-tests of presentations in order: (2) t(32) = –0.36, p=0.72; (3) t(32) = –3.55, p=0.001, Cohen's d=–0.62)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis.

claim: A t-test against 0 revealed significantly decreased activity in high-PP of the third presentation (t(32) = –2.92, p=0.006, Cohen's d=–0.51).
source: and a t-test against 0 revealed significantly decreased activity in high-PP of the third presentation (t(32) = –2.92, p=0.006, Cohen's d=–0.51).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis.

claim: EEG results indicate differences between PP conditions in desynchronization of alpha oscillations, as an assumed neural correlate of encoding depth.
source: In addition to the behavior results, these EEG results indicate differences between PP conditions in desynchronization of alpha oscillations, as an assumed neural correlate of encoding depth (Hanslmayr et al., 2009; Griffiths et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EEG results supported by citations.

claim: The conditions of high- and low-PP correspond to distinct levels in learning difficulty.
source: To summarize, as a manipulation check based on encoding analyses, we confirmed that the conditions of high- and low-PP correspond to distinct levels in learning difficulty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the encoding analyses.

claim: T-tests against 0 revealed a significant increase in the TMR/cueing condition of group 1 (high-PP cued: 0.24±0.1, t(10) = 2.44, p=0.035, Cohen's d=0.74).
source: Conducting t-tests against 0 revealed a significant increase in the TMR/cueing condition of group 1 (high-PP cued: 0.24±0.1, t(10) = 2.44, p=0.035, Cohen's d=0.74)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: Memory performance remained unchanged in the low-PP cued condition (–0.09±0.08, t(10) = –1.16, p=0.27).
source: while the memory performance remained unchanged in all the other conditions (low-PP cued: –0.09±0.08, t(10) = –1.16, p=0.27
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: Memory performance remained unchanged in the high-PP uncued condition (0±0.08, t(10) = –0.04, p=0.97).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: Memory performance remained unchanged in the low-PP uncued condition (0.03±0.1, t(10) = 0.31, p=0.76).
source: low-PP uncued: 0.03±0.1, t(10) = 0.31, p=0.76; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: A two-way mixed design ANOVA revealed trends of significance (p<0.1) for the interaction (cueing ×group: F(1,20) = 3.47, p=0.08).
source: An additional two-way mixed design ANOVA on the same values with the factor cueing (cued vs. uncued) as a within-subject factor and group as a between-subject factor revealed trends of significance (p<0.1) for the interaction (cueing ×group: F(1,20) = 3.47, p=0.08)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: A two-way mixed design ANOVA revealed trends of significance for the main effect of group (F(1,20) = 3.28, p=0.09).
source: and the main effect of group (F(1,20) = 3.28, p=0.09).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: The main effect of cueing was not significant (F(1,20) = 0.58, p=0.46).
source: The main effect of cueing was not significant (F(1,20) = 0.58, p=0.46).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the overnight memory change analysis.

claim: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed a significant difference between the conditions of high-PP-cued and low-PP-cued (t(20) = 2.63, p=0.02, Cohen's d=1.12).
source: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed a significant difference between the conditions of high-PP-cued and low-PP-cued (t(20) = 2.63, p=0.02, Cohen's d=1.12)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis of overnight memory changes.

claim: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed a trend of significance between high-PP-cued and high-PP-uncued (t(20) = 1.91, p=0.07).
source: a trend of significance between high-PP-cued and high-PP-uncued (t(20) = 1.91, p=0.07)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis of overnight memory changes.

claim: There was no significant difference between high-PP-cued and low-PP-uncued (t(10) = 1.55, p=0.15).
source: and no significant difference between high-PP-cued and low-PP-uncued (t(10) = 1.55, p=0.15).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis of overnight memory changes.

claim: Pre-sleep memory performance and vigilance shortly before the post-sleep memory task did not significantly differ between both cueing groups.
source: In additional control analyses, pre-sleep memory performance and vigilance shortly before the post-sleep memory task did not significantly (p-values ≥0.08) differ between both cueing groups (see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from control analyses.

claim: A significant overnight increase in c-criterion was found for cued sequences in group 1 (high-PP cued: 0.2±0.07, t(10) = 3.04, p=0.01, Cohen's d=0.92).
source: Here, we found as well a significant overnight increase for cued sequences in group 1 (high-PP cued: 0.2±0.07, t(10) = 3.04, p=0.01, Cohen's d=0.92), indicating an increased bias towards risk avoidance by TMR (Figure 3b)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the c-criterion analysis.

claim: TMR increased bias towards risk avoidance in the high-PP cued condition.
source: indicating an increased bias towards risk avoidance by TMR
evidence: This is an interpretation of the c-criterion results.

claim: All other c-criterion conditions remained unchanged (high-PP uncued: 0.09±0.06, t(10) = 1.4, p=0.19; low-PP cued: 0.08±0.05, t(10) = 1.63, p=0.13; low-PP uncued: 0.03±0.05, t(10) = 0.56, p=0.59).
source: while all the other conditions remained unchanged (high-PP uncued: 0.09±0.06, t(10) = 1.4, p=0.19; low-PP cued: 0.08±0.05, t(10) = 1.63, p=0.13; low-PP uncued: 0.03±0.05, t(10) = 0.56, p=0.59).
evidence: These are statistical results from the c-criterion analysis.

claim: An ANOVA on c-criterion changes showed no significant effects (interaction cueing ×group: F(1,20) = 2.66, p=0.12; main effect cueing F(1,20) = 2.08, p=0.17; main effect group F(1,20) = 0.38, p=0.55).
source: An ANOVA on c-criterion changes showed no significant effects (interaction cueing ×group: F(1,20) = 2.66, p=0.12; main effect cueing F(1,20) = 2.08, p=0.17; main effect group F(1,20) = 0.38, p=0.55).
evidence: These are statistical results from the c-criterion analysis.

claim: The effectiveness of TMR depends on the level of difficulty in word learning.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of TMR depends on the level of difficulty in word learning, while auditory cueing during sleep increases the memory performance of the easy to learn words.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: Auditory cueing during sleep increases the memory performance of the easy to learn words.
source: while auditory cueing during sleep increases the memory performance of the easy to learn words.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: Auditory word presentations during NREM sleep led to broad high-amplitude oscillations, called slow waves (SW; 0.5–3 Hz).
source: By visual inspection of the signals, auditory word presentations during NREM sleep led to broad high-amplitude oscillations, called slow waves (SW; 0.5–3 Hz)
evidence: This is an observation from EEG data during sleep.

claim: Sleep spindle activity (9–16 Hz) with various amplitude occurred preferentially nested during the SW's up-state phase.
source: whereas sleep spindle activity (9–16 Hz) with various amplitude occurred preferentially nested during the SW's up-state phase (see for example traces Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an observation from EEG data during sleep shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Testing changes of SW density in time windows of 0.5 s revealed significant increases after stimulus onset in comparison to baseline (0–0.5 s: 49.73 ± 14.32%, t(21) = 3.47, p=0.002, Cohen's d=0.74).
source: Testing changes of SW density in time windows of 0.5 s, revealed significant increases after stimulus onset in comparison to baseline (Figure 4b; baseline period of –1.5–0 s before stimulus onset; t-tests against 0; 0–0.5 s: 49.73 ± 14.32%, t(21) = 3.47, p=0.002, Cohen's d=0.74
evidence: This is a statistical result from slow wave density analysis.

claim: Testing changes of SW density revealed significant increases after stimulus onset (0.5–1 s: 83.44 ± 14.97%, t(21) = 5.57, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.19).
evidence: This is a statistical result from slow wave density analysis.

claim: Testing changes of SW density revealed significant increases after stimulus onset (1.5–2 s: 40.33 ± 10.67%, t(21) = 3.78, p=0.001, Cohen's d=0.84).
evidence: This is a statistical result from slow wave density analysis.

claim: Comparisons between the TMR conditions of high- and low-PP showed no significant differences in SW density, SW amplitude, number of TMR presentations and other sleep parameters.
source: Additional comparisons between the TMR conditions of high- and low-PP showed no significant differences in SW density, SW amplitude, number of TMR presentations and other sleep parameters, but a trend of significance for REM sleep parameters (see Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sleep parameter comparisons.

claim: There was a trend of significance for REM sleep parameters between TMR conditions.
source: but a trend of significance for REM sleep parameters (see Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sleep parameter comparisons.

claim: TMR increases SW in response to auditory word stimulation independent of difficulty in word learning.
source: In sum, these results indicate an increase of SW in response to auditory word stimulation independent of difficulty in word learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the slow wave density analysis.

claim: Fast spindle band activity (12–16 Hz) nested during SW up-states displayed a topography with maximum power over the central-parietal electrodes.
source: Figure 4c shows the grand average analyses per condition, whereas the fast spindle band activity (12–16 Hz) nested during SW up-states displayed a topography with maximum power over the central-parietal electrodes.
evidence: This is an observation from time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Comparison between PP conditions revealed a significant greater spindle-band power prominent in the frequency range of 11–14 Hz during SW up-states (from 0.3 to 0.8 s after the SW trough) of high- in contrast to low-PP (averaged t-value over the 5 cluster electrodes = 2.66, p=0.01, Cohen's d=1.13).
source: Comparison between PP conditions revealed a significant greater spindle-band power prominent in the frequency range of 11–14 Hz during SW up-states (from 0.3 to 0.8 s after the SW trough) of high- in contrast to low-PP (averaged t-value over the 5 cluster electrodes = 2.66, p=0.01, Cohen's d=1.13; Figure 4d)
evidence: This is a statistical result from cluster-based permutation analysis of spindle power.

claim: Post-hoc comparison including the individual SW amplitude as a covariate still revealed the significance of the spindle power cluster (t(20) = 2.38, p=0.03, Cohen's d=1.02).
source: whereas post-hoc comparison including the individual SW amplitude as a covariate still revealed the significance of this cluster (t(20) = 2.38, p=0.03, Cohen's d=1.02).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc analysis controlling for SW amplitude.

claim: Fast sleep spindles during the SW up-states occurred with significantly higher amplitude after the cueing presentation of high- compared to low-PP words.
source: By conducting an additional analyses based on detection of fast sleep spindles (12–16 Hz; see Methods), we confirmed that fast sleep spindles during the SW up-states (from 0.3 to 0.8 s after the SW trough) occurred with significantly higher amplitude after the cueing presentation of high- compared to low-PP words
evidence: This is a result from sleep spindle detection analysis.

claim: Parameters of sleep spindle density and the amount sleep spindles coupled to the SW up-state did not differ between the cueing conditions.
source: whereas parameters of sleep spindle density and the amount sleep spindles coupled to the SW up-state did not differed between the cueing conditions (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a result from sleep spindle detection analysis.

claim: Successful TMR of the easy to learn words is associated with increased spindle activity nested during SW up-states.
source: These results suggest that successful TMR of the easy to learn words is associated with increased spindle activity nested during SW up-states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spindle power analysis.

claim: Whole sample correlation analyses between the individual spindle power values of the significant cluster and the overnight changes of behavior measurements revealed no significant correlations (Δ d': r=0.16, p=0.48; Δ c-criterion: r=0.19, p=0.40).
source: Whereas we found a significant group difference in spindle power nested during SW up-states, conducting further whole sample (n=22) correlation analyses between the individual spindle power values of the significant cluster and the overnight changes of behavior measurements revealed no significant correlations (Δ d': r=0.16, p=0.48; Δ c-criterion: r=0.19, p=0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: This is the first study to address the critical role of learning difficulty by experimental manipulations of phonotactical word properties on TMR's effectiveness and its neural signatures.
source: To our knowledge, we present here the first study to address the critical role of learning difficulty by experimental manipulations of phonotactical word properties on TMR's effectiveness and its neural signatures.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Previous research in object association learning showed beneficial influences of encoding depth on TMR.
source: Related to our finding of TMR's effectiveness of the easy words, previous research in object association learning showed beneficial influences of encoding depth Creery et al., 2015
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Previous research in object association learning showed beneficial influences of prior knowledge on TMR.
source: and prior knowledge Groch et al., 2017 on TMR.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Prior knowledge affected sleep dependent memory integration of new words in children.
source: Language studies without using TMR revealed that prior knowledge affected sleep dependent memory integration of new words in children James et al., 2017
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: The complementary systems approach model proposes that new word memory temporarily encoded in the hippocampus transfers during sleep into cortical structures of lexical and phonological memory for long-term embedding, due to co-activation of both memory systems.
source: To explain these critical influences on consolidation during sleep, the model of the complementary systems approach of word learning (CLS; Davis and Gaskell, 2009) proposes that new word memory temporary encoded in the hippocampus transfer during sleep into cortical structures of lexical and phonological memory for long-term embedding, due to co-activation of both memory systems.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the CLS model.

claim: Word memory reactivation and consolidation during sleep depend on the hippocampal encoding depth and the cortical prior knowledge in phonotactics.
source: Thus, word memory reactivation and consolidation during sleep depend on the hippocampal encoding depth and the cortical prior knowledge in phonotactics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CLS model.

claim: Facilitated systems co-activation/consolidation of the easy to learn words by auditory cueing during sleep occurs via enhanced initial encoding and higher similarity to pre-existing phonotactical knowledge compared to the difficult to learn words.
source: Regarding our results, we suggest facilitated systems co-activation/consolidation of the easy to learn words by auditory cueing during sleep as a manipulation of both factors – via enhanced initial encoding and higher similarity to pre-existing phonotactical knowledge – compared to the difficult to learn words.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study results in the context of the CLS model.

claim: A very high degree of similarity might lead to a strong memory formation during wake-encoding, which could prevent an additional effect of consolidation during sleep.
source: To explain this discrepancy, we could speculate that a very high degree of similarity led to a strong memory formation during wake-encoding, which prevented an additional effect of consolidation during sleep.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for discrepant findings.

claim: Learned object-location associations only benefited from TMR during sleep when not almost perfectly recalled during prior wake.
source: Indeed, Creery et al., 2015 showed that learned object-location associations only benefited from TMR during sleep when not almost perfectly recalled during prior wake.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: A moderate encoding depth might benefit most from subsequent sleep consolidation compared to insufficient or almost perfect encoding.
source: Here, a moderate encoding depth might benefit most from subsequent sleep consolidation compared to insufficient or almost perfect encoding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited findings.

claim: TMR not only captures specific memory traces of the words and their reward associations, but also decision-making tendencies.
source: This observation suggests that TMR not only captures specific memory traces of the words and their reward associations, but also decision-making tendencies.
evidence: This is an inference from the c-criterion results.

claim: Ai et al. revealed altered reward-relevant decision preferences by TMR.
source: In a previous study, Ai et al., 2018 revealed altered reward-relevant decision preferences by TMR.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: The active system consolidation hypothesis proposes slow wave – sleep spindle coupling activities as an underlying mechanism of systems consolidation.
source: Accordingly, the active system consolidation hypothesis proposes slow wave – sleep spindle coupling activities as an underlying mechanism of systems consolidation (Rasch and Born, 2013; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Klinzing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies reported associations of SW and spindle activities during sleep with the integration of new memories in pre-existing knowledge networks.
source: whereas previous studies reported associations of SW and spindle activities during sleep with the integration of new memories in pre-existing knowledge networks (Tamminen et al., 2010; Tamminen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies by implementing machine learning for EEG decoding revealed that classification accuracy of distinct memory categories peaked above chance level synchronized with SW-spindle coupling events.
source: Strikingly, recent studies by implementing machine learning for EEG decoding revealed that classification accuracy of distinct memory categories peaked above chance level synchronized with SW-spindle coupling events (Cairney et al., 2018; Schreiner et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The results support the assumption of SW-spindle activities as an underlying mechanism of memory reactivation during sleep by providing additional evidence to link successful TMR on behavior to increased spindle activity during SW up-states.
source: Here, our results support the assumption of SW-spindle activities as an underlying mechanism of memory reactivation during sleep by providing additional evidence to link successful TMR on behavior to increased spindle activity during SW up-states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results in the context of existing theory.

claim: Participants used their prior knowledge of frequently occurring word-sound patterns to facilitate learning.
source: These results suggest that participants used their prior knowledge of frequently occurring word-sound patterns to facilitate learning.
evidence: This is an inference from the encoding performance differences between high-PP and low-PP words.

claim: Processing of incoming words with high-PP might co-activate consistent schemata of prior word sound knowledge and thus may lead to facilitated memory integration and stabilization during encoding in comparison to processing of more inconsistent words with low-PP.
source: Regarding the framework of schema theory (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017), processing of incoming words with high-PP might co-activate consistent schemata of prior word sound knowledge and thus may lead to facilitated memory integration and stabilization during encoding in comparison to processing of more inconsistent words with low-PP.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on schema theory.

claim: The suppression of alpha oscillations over parietal and occipital electrodes represents a neural correlate of mnemonic functioning.
source: Consequently, we assume that the suppression of alpha oscillations over parietal and occipital electrodes represent a neural correlate of mnemonic functioning.
evidence: This is an inference from the EEG encoding results.

claim: Previous studies linked desynchronization of alpha oscillations to memory processing.
source: Accordingly, previous studies linked desynchronization of alpha oscillations to memory processing Hanslmayr et al., 2009; Klimesch et al., 2006
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A study of intracranial electrophysiology in epilepsy patients showed that neocortical alpha/beta desynchronization precede and predict fast hippocampal gamma activity during learning.
source: A study of intracranial electrophysiology in epilepsy patients (Griffiths et al., 2019b) showed that neocortical alpha/beta desynchronization precede and predict fast hippocampal gamma activity during learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Coupled neocortical alpha/beta desynchronization and hippocampal gamma activities represent hippocampal-cortical information transfer important for memory formation.
source: The authors propose that these coupled activities represent hippocampal-cortical information transfer important for memory formation.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the cited study.

claim: Cortical alpha desynchronization is a neural marker of wake mnemonic processing according to distinct levels of difficulty in word learning.
source: Here, our findings let suggest cortical alpha desynchronization as neural marker of wake mnemonic processing according to distinct levels of difficulty in word learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the encoding EEG results.

claim: Studies linked alpha desynchronization to cognitive effort and cognitive load.
source: Additional studies linked alpha desynchronization to cognitive effort and cognitive load (Proskovec et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Alpha desynchronization is associated with memory across different tasks, modalities and experimental phases of encoding and retrieval.
source: On the other hand numerous studies investigating oscillatory correlates of learning and memory showed that alpha desynchronization is associated with memory across different tasks, modalities and experimental phases of encoding and retrieval (Hanslmayr et al., 2009; Griffiths et al., 2021; Michelmann et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2019b; Griffiths et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Griffiths et al. revealed by simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings a negative correlation between the occurrence of patterns of stimulus-specific information detected by fMRI and cortical alpha/beta suppression.
source: Strikingly, Griffiths et al., 2019a revealed by simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings a negative correlation between the occurrence of patterns of stimulus-specific information detected by fMRI and cortical alpha/beta suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: A decrease of alpha/beta oscillations might represent the neuronal mechanism of unmasking the task-critical signal by simultaneous suppression of task-irrelevant neuronal activities to promote information processing.
source: Here, the authors suggested that a decrease of alpha/beta oscillations might represent the neuronal mechanism of unmasking the task-critical signal by simultaneous suppression of task-irrelevant neuronal activities to promote information processing.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation from the cited study.

claim: Over the course of learning, elevated memory processing of the easier to learn stimuli is associated with enhanced information processing and thus accompanied by higher cortical alpha desynchronization in comparison to the more difficult to learn stimuli.
source: Following this interpretation, we assume that over the course of learning elevated memory processing of the easier to learn stimuli is associated with enhanced information processing and thus accompanied by higher cortical alpha desynchronization in comparison of the more difficult to learn stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's alpha desynchronization findings.

claim: The study has limitations due to a small sample size and between-subject comparisons.
source: Our study has limitations due to a small sample size and between-subject comparisons.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: The criteria of data analyses were not pre-registered.
source: The criteria of data analyses were not pre-registered
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of methodological limitation.

claim: The p-values of behavior analyses were not corrected for multiple comparisons.
source: and the p-values of our behavior analyses were not corrected for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of statistical limitation.

claim: Potential influences of phonotactic word properties and the prior encoding depth on TMR cannot be interpreted independently because the conditions of phonotactic word properties impacted already the encoding depth before sleep.
source: Further, potential influences of phonotactic word properties and the prior encoding depth on TMR cannot be interpreted independently because the conditions of phonotactic word properties impacted already the encoding depth before sleep.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a confound in the experimental design.

claim: Future studies could include a higher number of encoding trials for the low-PP words to equalize the encoding depth between conditions prior to TMR.
source: To disentangle these potential factors, future studies could include a higher number of encoding trials for the low-PP words to equalize the encoding depth between conditions prior to TMR, as successfully shown in a recent study (Cordi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on a cited study.

claim: A within-subject design with a larger sample size would provide a more robust control of interindividual differences in sleep and cognition.
source: Additionally, a within-subject design with a larger sample size would provide a more robust control of interindividual differences in sleep and cognition.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Parameters of sleep, the pre-sleep memory performance and the vigilance shortly before the post-sleep memory test revealed no significant group differences.
source: To control for potential confounders despite the influence of difficulty in word learning on TMR, we compared parameters of sleep, the pre-sleep memory performance and the vigilance shortly before the post-sleep memory test, revealing no significant group differences (see Supplementary files 3 and 5).
evidence: This is a result from control analyses.

claim: Other individual trait factors such as individual susceptibility to TMR might have differed between the groups.
source: Nevertheless, we cannot rule out that other individual trait factors differed between the groups, such as the individual susceptibility to TMR.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential confounds.

claim: Future research should replicate the study by conducting a within-subject design with cueing of subsets of previously learned low- and high-PP words providing all conditions within the same individuals.
source: To rule out these alternative explanations based on individual factors, we suggest for future research to replicate our study by conducting a within-subject design with cueing of subsets of previously learned low- and high-PP words providing all conditions within the same individuals as shown in other TMR studies (Schreiner and Rasch, 2015; Cairney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on cited studies.

claim: Language differences of pronunciation and phoneme structures might affect word perception and memory processing.
source: Further, we used artificial words based on American English in combination with German speaking participants, whereas language differences of pronunciation and phoneme structures might affect word perception and memory processing (Bohn and Best, 2012).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation supported by citation.

claim: English and German are considered to have the same language family.
source: On the other hand, both languages are considered to have the same language family (Eberhard et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: The phonological distance between English and German is quite short compared to Korean.
source: and the phonological distance between English and German is quite short compared for example to Korean (Luef and Resnik, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Major common phonological characteristics across English and German are preserved.
source: Thus, major common phonological characteristics across both languages are still preserved.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited information about language families.

claim: Behavior analyses revealed robust word discrimination learning and distinct memory performance according to different levels of phonotactic probabilities providing evidence of successful experimental manipulation.
source: In addition, our behavior analyses revealed robust word discrimination learning and distinct memory performance according to different levels of phonotactic probabilities providing evidence of successful experimental manipulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral results.

claim: The study investigated categorization learning of artificial words according to their reward associations (rewarded vs. unrewarded) and did not study aspects of generalization learning of artificial grammar rules.
source: Based on our paradigm, we investigated categorization learning of artificial words according to their reward associations (rewarded vs. unrewarded) and did not studied aspects of generalization learning of artificial grammar rules (Reber, 1967; Batterink and Paller, 2017; Batterink et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the scope of the study and distinguishes it from other paradigms.

claim: The difference in paradigm might limit the comparability between previous language-related studies and the current findings.
source: This difference might limit the comparability between these previous language-related studies and our findings.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in generalizability.

claim: The usage of artificial words with distinct phonotactical properties provided a successful way to manipulate learning difficulty and to investigate word properties on TMR.
source: However, the usage of artificial words with distinct phonotactical properties provided a successful way to manipulate learning difficulty and to investigate word properties on TMR
evidence: This is a conclusion about the methodological approach.

claim: The reward categorization learning paradigm had the advantage to increase the relevance of the word learnings due to incentives.
source: whereas our reward categorization learning paradigm had the advantage to increase the relevance of the word learnings due to incentives.
evidence: This is a justification for the methodological choice.

claim: Future research and clinical applications to restore language capabilities should consider learning difficulty based on phonotactical word properties as a potential factor of successful TMR.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that future research and clinical applications to restore language capabilities should consider learning difficulty based on phonotactical word properties as a potential factor of successful TMR
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Alpha desynchronization during initial learning – as a neural marker of encoding depth – may serve as a predictor for sleep-associated memory reactivation and consolidation.
source: whereas alpha desynchronization during initial learning – as a neural marker of encoding depth – may serve as a predictor for sleep-associated memory reactivation and consolidation.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the study findings.

claim: The study included 39 subjects (29 females) with an age range of 19–28 years (M=22.28 years, SD = 2.04).
source: The study included 39 subjects (29 females) with an age range of 19–28 years (M=22.28 years, SD = 2.04).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: All participants were German speakers.
source: All participants were German speakers
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: No subject had a history of neurological or psychiatric illness.
source: and no subject had a history of neurological or psychiatric illness.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria.

claim: Data were excluded from subjects who did not reach the minimal learning performance of d'>1.05 during the pre-sleep memory test in at least one of the two PP conditions (n=5).
source: Data were excluded from subjects who did not reach the minimal learning performance of d'>1.05 during the pre-sleep memory test in at least one of the two PP conditions, whereas this threshold value corresponds to accuracy rates of 70% (n=5).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria.

claim: One subject who showed a negative d' in one PP condition of the pre-sleep memory test was excluded (n=1).
source: In addition, we excluded one subject who showed a negative d' in one PP condition of the pre-sleep memory test (n=1).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria.

claim: The encoding task contained 480 trials in randomized order according to 160 artificial words with three presentations each.
source: The learning task contained 480 trials in randomized order according to 160 artificial words with three presentations each.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The memory task contains 160 trials according to the 160 artificial words.
source: The memory task contains 160 trials according to the 160 artificial words.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: All night sleep periods started with light off between 23:00 and 24:00 hr.
source: All night sleep periods started with light off between 23:00 and 24:00 hr.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Artificial words were presented aurally via loudspeakers (sound pressure level 55 dB) with a randomized inter-stimulus interval of 8±2 s during N2 and N3 sleep.
source: Based on online monitoring of N2 and N3 sleep, artificial words were presented aurally via loudspeakers (sound pressure level 55 dB) with a randomized inter-stimulus interval of 8±2 s.
evidence: This describes the TMR procedure.

claim: Word presentations were interrupted when an arousal or patterns of REM sleep were observed online.
source: We interrupted word presentations when we observed online an arousal or patterns of REM sleep.
evidence: This describes the TMR procedure.

claim: Phonotactic probability values were computed for each word using an online computation platform according to an American English lexicon.
source: Phonotactic probability values were computed for each word by using an online computation platform (Aljasser and Vitevitch, 2018) (https://calculator.ku.edu/phonotactic/English/words) according to an American English lexicon.
evidence: This describes the method for computing phonotactic probabilities.

claim: D'-values were calculated according to the signal detection theory (d'=z(hits)-z(false alarms)).
source: As a measurement of discrimination learning and memory performance, we calculated d'-values (d'=z(hits)-z(false alarms)) according to the signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This describes the behavioral analysis method.

claim: Response bias was assessed using c-criterion values (c=−0.5*(z(false alarms)+z(hits))).
source: In addition, we assessed measurements of the response bias (c=−0.5*(z(false alarms)+z(hits))).
evidence: This describes the behavioral analysis method.

claim: The final sample for sleep analyses consisted of n=22 with 11 subjects in each cueing condition.
source: The final sample for sleep analyses consisted of n=22 with 11 subjects in each cueing condition.
evidence: This describes the sample for sleep EEG analyses.

claim: The 30% slow waves with the highest amplitude were included for each subject in subsequent analyses.
source: To control for individual differences, we included 30% of SW with the highest amplitude per subject (see methods) in subsequent analyses.
evidence: This describes the slow wave selection criteria.

claim: A two-way mixed design ANOVA on the amplitude size of the sleep spindles showed a significant interaction effect (cueing group ×SW-coupling: F(1,20) = 4.51, p=0.046, η2=0.18).
source: A two-way mixed design ANOVA on the amplitude size of the sleep spindles with the cueing group as a between-subject factor (high-PP-cued vs. low-PP-cued) and SW-coupling as a within-subject factor (coupled vs. uncoupled) showed a significant interaction effect (cueing group ×SW-coupling: F(1,20) = 4.51, p=0.046, η2=0.18)
evidence: This is a statistical result from sleep spindle analysis.

claim: A two-way mixed design ANOVA on the amplitude size of the sleep spindles showed a significant main effect of SW-coupling (F(1,20) = 85.02, p<0.001, η2=0.81).
source: a significant main effect of SW-coupling (F(1,20) = 85.02, p<0.001, η2=0.81)
evidence: This is a statistical result from sleep spindle analysis.

claim: A two-way mixed design ANOVA on the amplitude size of the sleep spindles showed a trend of significance of the main effect of the cueing group (F(1,20) = 3.54, p=0.08).
source: and a trend of significance of the main effect of the cueing group (F(1,20) = 3.54, p=0.08).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sleep spindle analysis.

claim: Post-hoc unpaired t-tests revealed a significant higher amplitude size of the coupled sleep spindles of the cueing group of high- compared to low-PP (t(20) = 2.13, p=0.046, Cohen's d=0.91).
source: Post-hoc unpaired t-tests revealed a significant higher amplitude size of the coupled sleep spindles of the cueing group of high- compared to low-PP (t(20) = 2.13, p=0.046, Cohen's d=0.91; Figure 4—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc sleep spindle analysis.

claim: There was no significant group difference of the uncoupled sleep spindles (t(20) = 1.62, p=0.12).
source: and no significant group difference of the uncoupled sleep spindles (t(20) = 1.62, p=0.12).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc sleep spindle analysis.

claim: An additional comparison of the amount of coupled sleep spindles between the cueing groups revealed no significant difference.
source: An additional comparison of the amount of coupled sleep spindles between the cueing groups revealed no significant difference (see Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sleep spindle analysis.

claim: Detected sleep spindles coupled to the SW up-state phase occurred with higher amplitude after TMR presentations of the high-PP words in comparison to the low-PP words.
source: Here, we found that detected sleep spindles coupled to the SW up-state phase occurred with higher amplitude after TMR presentations of the high-PP words in comparison to the low-PP words
evidence: This is a conclusion from the sleep spindle detection analysis.

claim: The sleep spindle density and the amount of sleep spindles coupled to the SW up-state phase did not differ between the cueing conditions.
source: whereas the sleep spindle density and the amount of sleep spindles coupled to the SW up-state phase did not differed between the cueing conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the sleep spindle detection analysis.
